title: The greatest architect you’ve never heard of is in Pakistan - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Works in Progress profiles Lahore architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a London-trained former modernist who, after reading Nader Ardalan's work on Sufi Persian architecture in 1980, devoted decades to reviving Pakistan's traditional building with surviving hereditary craftsmen. The piece argues he may be among the world's best architects, overlooked abroad, and that craft-skill loss is the key constraint on traditional architecture everywhere.

insights.claim: Works in Progress suggests Pakistani architect Kamil Khan Mumtaz may be the world's best living architect, overlooked internationally mainly because global architecture magazines rarely cover Lahore.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reputation and recognition in architecture are skewed by where global media looks; under-covered geographies can hide top-tier talent.
insights.quote: overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore
insights.locator: Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood

insights.claim: Most of the portfolio of Kamil Khan Mumtaz's work published by Works in Progress, prepared by his assistant Sohaib Ahmed, had never before been seen outside Pakistan.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Signals an information gap that publishers can exploit by surfacing non-Western work to global audiences.
insights.locator: Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed

insights.claim: Kamil Khan Mumtaz trained at London's Architectural Association in the early 1960s, absorbing a standard modernist approach uncritically, and practiced as a resolutely modernist (and communist) architect in Pakistan after 1966.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Illustrates how elite Western training exported modernism as the default to post-colonial architects.
insights.quote: I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.

insights.claim: Mumtaz's early modernist workers' housing at Kot Karamat used arched roofs alien to rural Pakistani housing, which residents disliked because they preferred flat roofs to sleep on during summer nights.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Design that ignores local climate and habits fails its users — a recurring critique of top-down modernist housing.

insights.claim: Nader Ardalan's book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture, given to Mumtaz in 1980, triggered his abandonment of modernism and turn to reviving Lahore's and Pakistan's traditional architectural languages.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A single intellectual input redirected a career; traditional-architecture revival often starts from rediscovered theory.
insights.quote: It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.

insights.claim: Mumtaz reports a large latent public appetite in Pakistan for traditional architecture, held back by a widespread belief that it can no longer be built because the craftsmen are gone.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Latent demand for traditional built forms suggests a market opportunity where supply-side craft capacity, not taste, is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.
insights.locator: In the decades since, Mumtaz has worked

insights.claim: The loss of craft skills is a global bottleneck for traditional architecture: even factory-prefabricated traditional elements need skilled installation, and without it details look clumsy, as with crudely bolted appliqué columns at Berlin's 1990s Quartier Schützenstraße.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Industrialized pastiche fails without skilled labor; craft training is the real input to quality traditional building.
insights.locator: The loss of craft skills is a problem

insights.claim: Pakistan's later industrialization meant premodern hereditary craft families had not entirely vanished when Mumtaz began, letting him recruit remnant craftsmen such as metalworker Muhammed Hafeez, whose ancestors were specialist metalworkers for generations.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Late-industrializing countries may retain craft capital that rich countries lost — a comparative advantage for high-craft construction.
insights.quote: immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen
insights.locator: This problem also exists in Pakistan

insights.claim: Working with craftsmen, Mumtaz's practice has rediscovered lost techniques including certain brickwork, the flat dome and muqarnas vaults, some reportedly not built for 300 years.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Lost building techniques can be recovered within a career when practice and craft co-evolve, implying craft loss is reversible.
insights.quote: “This has not been done for 300 years!”
insights.locator: Mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically

insights.claim: In the late 1970s Mumtaz wrote a report arguing for preservation of the Walled City of Lahore against bureaucrats who wanted it demolished for modern high-rises; it was saved and parts are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Heritage advocacy can redirect state redevelopment plans; preserved historic cores become lasting cultural and tourism assets.
insights.quote: pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings
insights.locator: He also became involved in architectural conservation

insights.claim: Mumtaz's traditional approach spans homes, offices (including Oxford University Press in Karachi), mosques and schools, and has proven adaptable even to a tight-budget school for Lahore's Christian community.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shows traditional craft architecture is not limited to luxury commissions; it can be adapted to institutional and budget-constrained projects.
insights.locator: A school for Lahore’s Christian community

insights.claim: Now in his mid-eighties, Mumtaz remains uncertain whether his work has founded a lasting alternative approach to contemporary urban environments.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Whether the traditional revival outlives its founder is an open question — succession of craft networks is the key risk.
insights.quote: I’m just keeping my fingers crossed! No idea what will happen
